cases.title: Healthier people. Better insurance?
cases.question: Does having insurance explain why insured people report better health?
cases.story: A health survey can reveal a striking gap without telling us what caused it. The 2009 National Health Interview Survey asked people about their health, insurance, and household circumstances. This teaching extract selects married adults ages 26–59 in households with an employed adult; it is not a picture of every American. Each row records one person, including a self-reported health score, schooling, and family income. Insurance was not randomly assigned. People with coverage may also have jobs, resources, or other advantages that shape their health. Start by comparing health distributions, then look at who belongs to each insurance group. The question becomes more interesting as the comparison becomes less simple: if the groups differ in several ways, how could we separate the contribution of insurance from those other differences?
cases.takeaway: Compare health distributions, then look for differences that make a causal interpretation difficult.
cases.prediction: If insured people report better health, what are two explanations besides an effect of insurance?
cases.caution: Health is an ordered response from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), not a clinical measurement. This selected household sample is not the entire NHIS. Initial summaries give each row equal weight.
cases.bridge: What would random assignment of insurance change about the comparison you just made?
cases.source: National Center for Health Statistics, 2009 NHIS data release
cases.unit: Person in a selected sample of married adults ages 26–59 in households with an employed adult.

preview.caption: Describe where each distribution is concentrated. A health gap is an association; the chart does not tell us why coverage and health differ.

cases.title: Before the experiment begins
cases.question: Were people assigned to different insurance plans comparable at baseline?
cases.story: Imagine trying to learn whether free medical care improves health. Comparing people who buy different plans would mix the effects of insurance with the reasons they chose those plans. The RAND Health Insurance Experiment took a different approach: families were randomly assigned to plans with different cost-sharing arrangements. This file contains baseline characteristics from the experiment, including age, schooling, income, and health measures. Each row is a participant, while family members share an assignment and may resemble one another. Before examining later outcomes, we can ask whether the plan groups started out looking similar. Random assignment does not guarantee identical averages in a finite sample, and missing records can complicate the picture. This investigation develops the habit of checking the starting point before interpreting an apparent treatment effect.
cases.takeaway: Look for baseline similarities and differences across plans, while keeping missing records visible.
cases.prediction: Would random assignment make every plan group have exactly the same average age? Why?
cases.caution: Plan type is missing for some stored rows. Comparisons use only known plan types and available values for the plotted outcome. Participants within a family are not independent assignments.
cases.bridge: Why does an outcome difference become more informative when the groups were comparable before treatment?
cases.source: Aron-Dine, Einav and Finkelstein (2013), The RAND Health Insurance Experiment, Three Decades Later

cases.title: When care costs less, do people use more?
cases.question: How does healthcare use differ across randomly assigned insurance plans?
cases.story: An insurance plan changes the price a family faces when someone needs care. Lower prices may encourage useful treatment, but they can also increase spending without producing equal improvements in health. The RAND experiment assigned families to plans ranging from free care to substantial cost sharing. This extract joins healthcare-use records and annual spending, with expenses expressed in constant 1991 dollars. A row represents a participant-year, so the same person can contribute more than one record. Most people may spend relatively little while a small number incur very large expenses. That makes this a useful case for learning why a mean alone can be misleading. We will inspect the distribution, compare visits across plans, and ask what a spending difference does—and does not—tell us about the value of medical care.
cases.takeaway: Explore skewed spending and compare visits and expenses across plans.
cases.prediction: Could two plans have similar typical spending but quite different average spending?
cases.caution: Rows are participant-years. Spending is in constant 1991 dollars. Repeated people and family assignments matter for inference; this lesson makes descriptive comparisons only.
cases.bridge: If free care increases visits, what additional outcomes would you need to decide whether it improves health?
cases.source: Aron-Dine, Einav and Finkelstein (2013), The RAND Health Insurance Experiment, Three Decades Later
cases.unit: Participant-year after inner joining claims and annual spending.

cases.title: More care. Better health?
cases.question: How do measured health outcomes compare across insurance plans?
cases.story: Using more healthcare and becoming healthier are different outcomes. The RAND Health Insurance Experiment makes that distinction tangible: families were assigned different cost-sharing plans, and researchers collected health measures as well as spending records. This extract contains exit measures such as a general health index, blood pressure, and cholesterol. A row represents a participant in the stored exit-measure file, but some rows lack the measurements needed for a particular comparison. Different outcomes also have different scales and interpretations; higher values are not always better. We will first make the available evidence visible, then compare the distributions of selected health measures across plans. The aim is to learn how to ask a precise outcome question and avoid turning one descriptive chart into a broad claim about every participant or every dimension of health.
cases.takeaway: Compare health outcomes and check whether missing measurements limit the comparison.
cases.prediction: If a plan produces more medical visits, must it improve every health measure?
cases.caution: Outcome availability differs across measures. Do not combine health indices, blood pressure, and cholesterol on one numeric scale. These plots are not clinical advice or estimates of statistical significance.
cases.bridge: How could missing exit measurements weaken a comparison that began with random assignment?
cases.source: Aron-Dine, Einav and Finkelstein (2013), The RAND Health Insurance Experiment, Three Decades Later
cases.unit: RAND HIE participant with exit health measures.

cases.title: Assigned is not always delivered
cases.question: When officers were assigned a response, how often was that response delivered?
cases.story: In Minneapolis in 1981–1982, researchers studied police responses to eligible misdemeanor domestic assault incidents. Officers were assigned one of three responses: arrest, advice, or separating the parties. The wider study asked whether these responses affected repeat violence. In practice, an assigned response was not always the response delivered. This teaching extract contains 314 records with only those two categorical fields; the original study involved 330 cases, and the extract does not contain subsequent violence outcomes. We can therefore investigate how assignment translated into action, but cannot estimate whether arrest reduced repeat violence from this file. A count chart and a cross-tabulation make the distinction visible. It is a concrete introduction to noncompliance: even when an assignment is randomized, the treatment actually received may reflect additional decisions and circumstances.
cases.takeaway: Trace the difference between assigned and delivered responses, then identify the evidence still missing.
cases.prediction: Would comparing people actually arrested with people not arrested preserve the original random assignment?
cases.caution: This extract has no recidivism outcome. Its 314 records must not be described as all 330 study cases. Use respectful language: these records concern serious harm to people.
cases.bridge: Why might assigned response be a more credible starting point than delivered response when investigating an arrest effect?
cases.source: Sherman and Berk (1984), The Minneapolis Domestic Violence Experiment
cases.unit: Police response to an eligible misdemeanor domestic assault call (330 cases in source study).

definitions.assigned: Police response assigned by the experiment: Arrest, Advise, or Separate.
definitions.delivered: Police response actually delivered; compare its category label with assigned.

preview.question: For each assigned response, what was actually delivered?
preview.caption: Off-diagonal cells show noncompliance. A comparison based on delivered responses can therefore sort cases differently from the randomized assignment.

cases.title: What changes on a twenty-first birthday?
cases.question: Do mortality patterns change at the age when alcohol becomes legally available?
cases.story: A birthday is an ordinary passage of time, but turning 21 in the United States also changes legal access to alcohol. Carpenter and Dobkin used this threshold to investigate the relationship between alcohol access and mortality. The teaching file records mortality rates for narrow age cells around the cutoff rather than individual people. Each point on a chart is therefore an aggregate, measured in deaths per 100,000 person-years. The file contains both actual age and age centered on 21; confusing the two would put the policy threshold in the wrong place. We will plot actual age, compare causes of death, and zoom in near the birthday. The central reasoning challenge is to distinguish a gradual age pattern from an abrupt change at the policy boundary, while asking what else could change at precisely the same age.
cases.takeaway: Use an age threshold to ask when nearby observations might offer a useful comparison.
cases.prediction: Would you expect mortality to change smoothly with age, or jump at a particular birthday?
cases.caution: Use agecell for actual age; age is centered on 21. Rates describe age cells, not individual death probabilities. A visible jump alone does not establish the assumptions of a causal design.
cases.bridge: What must be true about other influences near age 21 for the cutoff to help isolate legal alcohol access?
cases.source: Carpenter and Dobkin (2009), The Effect of Alcohol Consumption on Mortality

definitions.agecell: Actual age in years for an aggregate mortality cell.
definitions.age: Age centered on 21: actual age minus 21, in years. Use agecell for actual age.
definitions.over21: Indicator for the age-21 cutoff side: 1 at or above the threshold.

preview.caption: A local change suggests a question for regression discontinuity. Whether it identifies an alcohol-access effect depends on other influences being sufficiently smooth at the boundary.

cases.title: Two districts. One banking crisis.
cases.question: Did different Federal Reserve responses help banks survive the Great Depression?
cases.story: During the Great Depression, Mississippi straddled two Federal Reserve districts that responded differently to banking distress. Richardson and Troost studied this boundary to investigate whether emergency lending helped banks survive. This teaching extract gives six July 1 snapshots of the number of banks still in business in each district. These are operating-bank counts, not counts of failures, and the districts did not start with the same number of banks. The file also supplies a constructed path for the sixth district based on the eighth district’s changes from 1930. That path is a counterfactual illustration, not another observed district. By looking first at levels and then at changes, we can ask why a before-and-after comparison might be insufficient and what a comparison district contributes to the argument. Six observations are enough for an important question, but not for unlimited historical conclusions.
cases.takeaway: Compare changes in operating banks and separate observed history from a constructed counterfactual.
cases.prediction: If both districts lose banks, could lending still have helped one district?
cases.caution: There are only six annual snapshots. bib6 and bib8 count banks in business. The supplied counterfactual holds the 1930 district gap fixed; it is not observed evidence of what would certainly have happened.
cases.bridge: What would make the eighth district a credible guide to how the sixth would have changed without intervention?
cases.source: Richardson and Troost (2009), Monetary Intervention Mitigated Banking Panics during the Great Depression
cases.unit: Annual July 1 snapshot of banks in business in each Federal Reserve district.

definitions.year: Calendar year of the observation; census year in the child-labor file.
definitions.bib6: Number of banks in business in the sixth Federal Reserve district on the July 1 snapshot.
definitions.bib8: Number of banks in business in the eighth Federal Reserve district on the July 1 snapshot.
definitions.counterfactual: Constructed sixth-district path holding the 1930 sixth–eighth district gap fixed; not observed.

preview.question: How many banks remained in business in each district?
preview.caption: Fewer operating banks is a decline in this count. It is not a direct count of failures, and the starting difference makes a simple level comparison uninformative about policy.

cases.title: A policy changes. A trend continues.
cases.question: How do drinking-age policy and young-adult mortality move across states and years?
cases.story: When states change a drinking-age law, many other things are changing too: road safety, travel, economic conditions, and public attitudes. A state-by-year panel allows us to follow these overlapping changes rather than compare just two national averages. This prepared teaching extract contains death rates for young adults, a legal-access measure, and population information, repeated for several causes of death. Each row describes one state, year, and cause, not one person. The chapter identifies the population as ages 18–20, although the repository does not reproduce the entire upstream cleaning process. We will keep causes separate, follow selected state trajectories, and put policy changes alongside mortality trends. The point is to see why an apparent policy association raises further questions about timing and comparison groups before it becomes a causal claim.
cases.takeaway: Read a panel as repeated state observations and investigate policy timing without pooling incompatible outcomes.
cases.prediction: If mortality falls after a law changes, what other trend could explain the decline?
cases.caution: Select one dtype before averaging rates. legal measures the share legally allowed to drink, not a randomized binary assignment. Population weighting changes which states contribute most.
cases.bridge: How could states with different policy timing help distinguish a policy effect from a shared national trend?
cases.source: Chapter 5 MLDA teaching panel; Du Mouchel, Williams and Zador (1987), Raising the Alcohol Purchase Age: Its Effects on Fatal Motor Vehicle Crashes in Twenty-Six States
cases.unit: State × year × death cause, for the chapter’s ages 18–20 population.

definitions.state: State identifier. Empirical state-panel codes follow U.S. state coding; simulated state IDs have no real geography.
definitions.dtype: Cause of death: all (all causes), MVA (motor vehicles), suicide, or internal. Filter before averaging rates.
definitions.mrate: Mortality rate per 100,000 in the chapter’s ages 18–20 population.
definitions.legal: Share of the relevant age group legally allowed to drink, from 0 to 1.
definitions.pop: Population of the relevant state-year age group; chapter uses this as a population analysis weight.

cases.title: Can a birthday shape schooling?
cases.question: Why might quarter of birth be related to schooling, and what could that teach us about earnings?
cases.story: People with more schooling often earn more, but that pattern combines education with the reasons people stay in school. Angrist and Krueger investigated a different source of variation: birth timing interacting with school-entry and compulsory-attendance rules. This extract contains men from the 1980 U.S. Census, with schooling, log weekly earnings, and quarter and year of birth. It is the largest file in the collection, so plotting every person at once can conceal rather than reveal structure. We will begin with summaries that use all relevant rows, then compare birth-quarter patterns within cohorts. The differences may be small; reading their size carefully is part of the lesson. A birthday does not automatically become a valid instrument. The investigation ends by asking what assumptions connect birth timing, schooling, and earnings.
cases.takeaway: Discover a small schooling pattern within a large census extract and ask what would make it useful for causal reasoning.
cases.prediction: Would you expect people born in different quarters of the same year to have similar schooling?
cases.caution: lnw is log weekly earnings, not dollars. yob uses two-digit birth-year codes. Group means use all available rows; any display sample must be identified.
cases.bridge: Besides changing schooling, could quarter of birth be related to earnings through another route?
cases.source: Angrist and Krueger (1991), Does Compulsory School Attendance Affect Schooling and Earnings? Author data archive

definitions.lnw: Natural logarithm of weekly earnings; not dollar earnings.
definitions.qob: Quarter of birth: 1 January–March through 4 October–December.
definitions.yob: Year of birth; two-digit 1930s codes in qob_clean, full years in childlabor_clean.

preview.question: Are birth-quarter schooling differences visible within birth years?
preview.caption: A small schooling difference may motivate an instrument, but small differences also demand careful inference. Birth timing is not automatically random with respect to every earnings determinant.

cases.title: A comparison within the family
cases.question: Does the schooling–wage pattern look different when we compare twins?
cases.story: Comparing unrelated people leaves many possible explanations for a schooling–earnings association. Twins offer a way to hold some family background and inherited characteristics more nearly constant. The Twinsburg research collected information about education and wages, including reports of schooling from both twins. This prepared extract contains individual observations and supplied within-pair differences. It does not give us a general-purpose pair identifier, so we must follow the chapter’s instruction to use records marked first when examining those differences. We will contrast the individual pattern with a chart of schooling and wage differences within pairs, then inspect disagreement between schooling reports. Similar upbringing does not eliminate every difference between twins, and reported schooling can contain error. This case shows both the appeal of a closer comparison and the new questions it introduces.
cases.takeaway: Compare individuals with within-pair differences, and see why measurement quality matters.
cases.prediction: What influences on earnings might twins share, and what influences might still differ?
cases.caution: Use first == 1 once per pair for supplied differences. Do not infer pairs from row order. lwage and dlwage are log-wage quantities, not dollar wages.
cases.bridge: Why might removing shared background make measurement error in schooling differences more important?
cases.source: Twinsburg studies: Ashenfelter and Krueger (1994); Ashenfelter and Rouse (1998). Book replication resource
cases.unit: Individual twin within a twin pair.

definitions.lwage: Natural logarithm of wage in the twins source; not a dollar wage.
definitions.educt_t: Twin-reported education of the respondent, in years.
definitions.age2: Squared age term; uses centered age in the drinking-age file and actual age in the twins file.
definitions.first: Indicator selecting the first record per twin pair; use 1 for supplied pair differences.
definitions.dlwage: Supplied within-pair difference in log wages.
definitions.deduc: Supplied within-pair difference in own-reported years of education.
definitions.deduct: Supplied within-pair difference in twin-reported years of education.

preview.caption: Twins can differ in earnings even when schooling matches. Shared background is only one set of influences, and pair differences can contain measurement error.

cases.title: The variable you almost overlooked
cases.question: How can ability complicate the relationship between schooling and earnings?
cases.story: Real data rarely reveal every reason that people choose more education. This teaching simulation gives us an advantage: the data-generating code includes ability, schooling, occupation, and log earnings, so we can inspect relationships that might be hidden in practice. Each row is a simulated person. Ability influences both schooling and earnings, while occupation is partly a consequence of schooling and provides another route to earnings. These roles are different: a variable that precedes schooling is not interchangeable with one that follows it. We will start with the familiar schooling–earnings pattern, color observations by ability, and compare it with the schooling–occupation relationship. The numbers are generated for learning, not evidence about an actual population. Their value is that they let us reason explicitly about why adding a variable to an analysis can change what question we are answering.
cases.takeaway: Visualize a confounder and distinguish it from a variable that lies on a causal pathway.
cases.prediction: If ability raises both schooling and earnings, would the raw schooling–earnings pattern exaggerate the effect of schooling?
cases.caution: The column earnings contains simulated log earnings. Occupation is generated after schooling and acts as a mediator. The generator includes clipping and rounding, so simplistic exact-effect claims are inappropriate.
cases.bridge: Why might controlling for occupation remove part of the schooling effect you wanted to learn about?

definitions.schooling: Simulated completed years of schooling, clipped to 6–20 and rounded.

preview.caption: This is the visual signature of the confounding built into the simulation. Coloring points reveals a relationship; it does not statistically remove it.

cases.title: A scholarship offer changes the comparison
cases.question: What does randomized scholarship assignment reveal about schooling and earnings?
cases.story: Suppose a scholarship is offered by lottery. Recipients may spend longer in school, but they do not all acquire the same amount of education. This teaching simulation separates the randomized offer from the schooling that follows it. Each generated person has an ability score, a scholarship assignment, years of schooling, and log earnings. Ability affects schooling and earnings, while the scholarship changes schooling without being selected on ability. We will compare ability distributions across the lottery groups, examine how their schooling differs, and then inspect earnings. That sequence helps avoid a common leap: an effect of offering a scholarship is not automatically an effect per additional year of education. Because the relationships are constructed, this is a safe place to explore the logic before encountering the complications of a real experiment.
cases.takeaway: Follow a randomized offer through schooling and earnings, keeping assignment distinct from treatment received.
cases.prediction: Should scholarship recipients have systematically higher ability before receiving the offer?
cases.caution: This is simulated data, not an actual scholarship evaluation. earnings contains log earnings. Schooling is clipped and rounded by the generator.
cases.bridge: What additional assumptions would let a randomized scholarship offer help identify the effect of schooling itself?

definitions.ability: Simulated pre-existing ability score (standard normal in Chapter 6).
definitions.scholarship: Randomized simulated scholarship offer: 1 offered, 0 not offered.

preview.question: How do schooling distributions differ between lottery groups?
preview.caption: Scholarship assignment and schooling received are different variables. The distributional shift motivates a first-stage question in the chapter.

cases.title: When the law keeps children in school
cases.question: How do schooling and wages vary across cohorts exposed to different schooling requirements?
cases.story: School attendance is shaped by family circumstances as well as legal requirements. Acemoglu and Angrist studied historical schooling laws to investigate education and earnings. This teaching file is already aggregated: a row represents a birth-state, birth-year, and census-year cell, with average schooling and log weekly wages. The law indicators distinguish required-schooling categories associated with child-labor restrictions; they must not be interpreted as ages for entering school. This distinction matters because an appealing story can be wrong even when the code runs. We will compare cohort patterns and law categories while keeping the aggregate observation unit visible. States and cohorts differ in many ways besides laws, so these charts are a starting point for asking what variation might support an instrument, not a direct estimate of a law’s causal effect.
cases.takeaway: Read aggregate cells carefully and explore how legal requirements might create schooling variation.
cases.prediction: Would states with stricter schooling requirements necessarily be comparable in other ways?
cases.caution: cl7, cl8 and cl9 identify required-schooling categories (7, 8, and 9 or more years), not school-entry ages. weight is a source sample-line analysis weight; n is a stored cell count. Equal-cell summaries are explicitly unweighted.
cases.bridge: What differences between states and birth cohorts would need attention before treating a law as a source of causal variation?
cases.source: Acemoglu and Angrist (2000), How Large Are Human-Capital Externalities? Evidence from Compulsory Schooling Laws; author archive

cases.title: What is a diploma worth?
cases.question: Does crossing an exit-exam threshold change diploma receipt and later earnings?
cases.story: A diploma may signal skills to employers, but graduates also tend to have more schooling and different backgrounds than nongraduates. Clark and Martorell studied students near a Texas high-school exit-exam passing threshold to make a closer comparison. This extract contains score-bin averages rather than individual student records. Each bin records a diploma-receipt rate, average later earnings, and the number of students represented. Passing the exam does not translate perfectly into receiving a diploma, which makes it useful to examine the two links separately: score to credential, and score to earnings. We will mark the passing threshold, inspect both outcomes, and look at how much information supports each point. A large visual difference in a small bin deserves different scrutiny from a stable pattern supported by many students.
cases.takeaway: Separate passing an exam, receiving a diploma, and earning more, while checking bin sizes.
cases.prediction: Would a jump in diploma receipt necessarily imply a jump in earnings?
cases.caution: minscore is distance from the passing threshold. Each row is a score bin; n counts students, while person_years supports earnings observations. Do not average bins as though they were individual students.
cases.bridge: Why must a design first establish that crossing the threshold actually changes the probability of receiving a diploma?
cases.source: Clark and Martorell (2014), The Signaling Value of a High School Diploma

definitions.minscore: Last-chance exam score relative to the passing threshold (0).
definitions.pass_exam: Indicator for passing the exam threshold.
definitions.receivehsd: Proportion receiving a high-school diploma in the score bin, from 0 to 1.

cases.title: A reform arrives halfway through the story
cases.question: How do schooling and earnings trajectories differ around a simulated reform?
cases.story: A policy often arrives after years of change are already underway. This simulation follows 20 states from 1995 to 2014, with ten adopting a schooling reform in 2005. Each row is a state-year average. The generator gives states different starting levels, a shared underlying time trend, and random fluctuations; after adoption, it adds a schooling increase and a change in average log earnings to treated states. We will first inspect the trajectories, then compare schooling patterns and changes relative to a common pre-reform year. Looking at changes helps separate starting differences from subsequent movement. In this artificial world, we can inspect the assumptions written into the generator. In an actual policy study, we would have to argue for those assumptions using evidence and institutional knowledge rather than knowing them by construction.
cases.takeaway: Compare levels and changes, then explain the counterfactual role of the comparison states.
cases.prediction: If treated states start with lower earnings, does that alone make them an unsuitable comparison?
cases.caution: Rows are repeated state-years, not independent people. avg_earnings is an average log-earnings outcome. Similar pre-trends are evidence to consider, not proof of future parallel trends.
cases.bridge: What would threaten the claim that comparison states describe how treated states would have changed without reform?

definitions.state: State identifier. Empirical state-panel codes follow U.S. state coding; simulated state IDs have no real geography.
definitions.year: Calendar year of the observation; census year in the child-labor file.
definitions.treated: Indicator for simulated reform states 1–10 (1), versus comparison states 11–20 (0).
definitions.avg_schooling: Simulated state-year average years of schooling.
definitions.avg_earnings: Simulated state-year average log earnings, not dollars.

preview.caption: Parallel movement does not require equal levels. In this simulation the shared trend is imposed by the generator; real evidence cannot establish future parallel trends with certainty.
